The holiday has stopped the clock of the state, but not the hunger of the body. I will eat this simple food, for it is the universal necessity that binds us all, and then we must face the particular absurdity of my identity. Hegde is here, a witness to the mix-up, and the file sits on the table like a sleeping snake waiting to strike.
Ramesh, the paratha is excellent. Hegde, you see the situation: I am eating as Hegel, but the file expects Hegde. Let us open it and see what the Directorate demands of a man who is neither.

Ramesh is right to dismiss the anxiety; the name is a clerical accident, not an ontological crisis, yet the file must be resolved for the sake of order. I have finished the paratha, and the holiday silence outside makes the house feel too small for my thoughts. It is time to move.
Thank you, Ramesh. The file will wait for the Directorate, but my legs do not. I shall return before lunch.
Ji Sahib, the gate key is on the hook. Chai is ready whenever you get back.

The holiday silence is absolute, which is a strange kind of noise. I am walking among the tombs of the Lodis, Muslim kings who built these domes while the Hindu spirit, I believe, remains in a state of dreaming, unshackled by the state but also unfree in the true sense. The air is cool, fifteen degrees, a mercy compared to the noon heat. I shall walk the perimeter, observing how the universal order of the garden holds even when the particular citizens are absent.
Gardeners squat in a row at a flower bed and pull weeds by hand, dropping them into flat baskets they push ahead of them, a hose lying uncoiled on the path beside them.

The gardeners work in a line, a human chain of necessity moving through the green. It is the same motion as the state: the universal order sustained by the particular labor of individuals who do not question the whole, only the next weed. I watch them with a detached respect; they are the actuality of the garden's idea.
Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.

Sikandar Lodi's tomb is a plain octagon, severe and unadorned, standing inside its own high walled garden. The gravel bears the neat lines of a rake, a geometry imposed on the earth that mirrors the order of the state. It is a monument to a dynasty that ruled from this city, yet it sits in a garden that feels more like a private enclosure than a public space, a small, contained world within the larger silence of the holiday.

entries.text: The walk has settled me, but the air in the bungalow is still and the clock points to the hour of service. I cannot dine on the cold remnants of breakfast, nor can I face the German lesson on an empty stomach. I will wait for the food to be laid out, then eat quickly to be ready for Ananya.

The meal is laid out: kadhi, rice, aloo gobhi. Ramesh watches from the doorway, his face a mask of patient service. I eat, for the body must be sustained, but my mind is already elsewhere, on the road to Khan Market, where the civil system of needs continues its quiet commerce despite the holiday.
Ramesh, the food is good. Thank you. I shall rest a while after this, then I intend to walk to Khan Market.
Khan Market is a bit of a trek from here, Sahib. The sun is out, but the breeze is nice today. I will keep the chai warm in case you need it on the way back.

The meal is finished, and the clock shows 13:45. My plan for Khan Market is at 15:00, leaving me a full hour of quiet. I will use this time to sit with my thoughts and perhaps review the German lesson material for Ananya, ensuring the afternoon passes with purpose rather than mere waiting.

The afternoon light is sharp and the house is quiet, but I cannot settle into a nap with the identity query still hanging over me like a storm cloud. Ramesh is present, and I need to ask him directly if he has seen any official correspondence or if he knows the local procedures for rectifying a clerical error, as I cannot simply wait for the Directorate to correct their own mistake.

entries.text: Ramesh, sit for a moment. I have a question about the Directorate. If a man is allotted a house by mistake of name, how does he prove he is not the man named? Do I go back to their office, or is there a police station I must visit first? I need to know the form this error takes.
Sahib, I just keep the place clean, I don't know their office work. For a name mistake, you go to the CPWD office with your papers, or maybe a lawyer. I can't tell you which form to fill.

Ramesh is right; he is a caretaker, not a clerk, and his ignorance of the form is a fact, not an insult. I cannot solve the identity crisis with a broom. The lesson is at 17:00, and I have time to walk to Khan Market to find a distraction, perhaps a book, before the afternoon closes. The heat is mild, a clear sky, suitable for a stroll.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall manage the office work myself. Keep the house quiet.
Chalega, Sahib. The house will be as quiet as a tomb.
Hegel. You are late. The shop closes at twenty, and I am not staying to measure a man who wanders around like a ghost.

Masterji is sharp today, and rightly so; I have spent the morning in the abstract and the afternoon in the air, while he keeps his hours. The heat is broken by the shade of the market, and I am hungry enough to want something stronger than the chai Sunil is offering, but my wallet is thin and my schedule tight. I shall take a quick bite and leave before the shopkeeper’s patience, which is already wearing thin, snaps.
Masterji, you are right. I apologize for the delay. I will be quick. Sunil, a cup of chai, please.
Apology accepted, but time is not. You have twenty minutes before the shutters go up, so use them well.

Twenty minutes. The tailor's clock is more honest than the sun's; he does not negotiate with the light, only with the needle. I shall sit, let him measure the hem of this kurta, and perhaps ask for a postcard or a small book to fill the silence before the shutters fall. The air here is still warm, a residual heat that lingers like a memory in a cold room.

Masterji, your time is your own, and I respect the boundary of your day. I am merely passing, but I require a small alteration to this kurta—the hem sits a fraction too high. While you work, might I trouble you for a postcard? Or perhaps a book on local history, if your shelves extend to such things?
Hem is simple, I will fix it in ten minutes. No postcards here, only fabric and thread. If you want a book, go to the bookstall next door, I do not sell stories to men in hurry.

Masterji’s efficiency is a relief; the hem will be done while I am elsewhere. I have no time to browse for a postcard, and the lesson is in forty-eight minutes. I will take a cup of chai to steady my nerves before returning to the bungalow.
Thank you, Masterji. I will be back in a moment for the kurta. Sunil, one cup of chai, please.
Ten minutes. No more. And Sunil, make it strong, not that weak tea you gave him last time.

Masterji’s command is clear: the tea must be strong, and the time is short. I have forty-eight minutes before the lesson with Ananya, and the walk home takes ten. I shall sit here, drink this cup properly, and let the heat of the chai and the market’s noise settle the mind before I return to the house. The white kurta will be ready by evening, which is sufficient.

The hem is done, or will be, and the tea is in hand. I have thirty-eight minutes before the lesson, and the bookseller’s stall is still open. A postcard would be a small anchor, a way to say something to the world that is not a query to the Directorate. I shall browse quickly.

The market is thinning out, the holiday having done its work on the crowd. I have my tea and my errands are sorted, but the lesson at home awaits in forty-eight minutes. I must not be late for the young woman; punctuality is the first lesson in freedom, before the grammar begins.
Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh brings the tea and toast, a small act of service that bridges the gap between my need and his duty. The lesson with Ananya begins in one minute, so I must accept this sustenance quickly and with gratitude, for a clear head is required for the transmission of language and thought.
Thank you, Ramesh. It is most timely. I shall be ready for the lesson in a moment.
The lesson? You are getting quite the show, Sahib. I will just leave this here on the side table.
Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

The hour has come for the exchange of signs. Ananya is present, and Ramesh has placed the tray, a small ritual of hospitality that precedes instruction. I shall begin with the basics, establishing the framework of the language before we delve into its particularities. The heat has broken, making the air suitable for clear thinking.

shelf.ref: The Struggle of Enlightenment with Superstition

entries.text: Ananya, sit. We begin. The German tongue is precise; it does not allow for the vagueness of the East, though it is not yet the rigorous freedom of the West. Repeat after me: Ich bin.
Wait, seriously? 'Vagueness of the East'? That's a bit much for a first lesson. Anyway, I'm ready, I guess. Ich bin.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

The lesson is over, and the cash is in my pocket, a small victory in the economy of needs. Ananya’s reaction to my words on the East was expected; she is of this place, and the distance between our perspectives is the very friction that makes the lesson possible. I have a debt to pay and a body that needs rest before dinner. Ramesh is here, and the dhobi’s bill falls due tomorrow, but I must not forget the immediate administrative burden.

Ramesh, the lesson is finished. Please ensure the house is ready for dinner at half-past seven. Also, remind me that I must settle the dhobi's account tomorrow; I do not wish to have such minor matters lingering.
The dhobi is already settled, Sahib. You paid him in full this morning, so there is nothing to worry about. I will have the dinner table ready by half past seven.

Ramesh confirms the dhobi is settled, which clears one knot from the day's ledger. The table will be ready at 19:30, so I have an hour and a half to fill. The air is cool and clear, the best time for a walk, but the identity file still burns in my mind. I will take a brief rest to gather my thoughts before dinner.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall be ready for dinner.
Yes, Sahib. Just a moment.
Ramesh has gone to check the dining room. The air is still, and the quiet of the house settles in. I remain seated, watching the door, waiting for the next service of the day to be announced.

entries.text: The cool air of the December evening settles into the bones, a welcome contrast to the day's heat. I am seated in the drawing room, observing the quiet interplay of Ramesh's diligence and Hegde's bewildered presence. There is no movement to make, only the quiet accumulation of the evening's stillness before the meal is served.

Ramesh sets the table with rotis, palak paneer, and dal, the meal ready before he leaves for the night. I am hungry, having eaten three hours ago, and the cool air makes the warmth of the food welcome. I shall eat plainly, without ceremony, and then retire to my books.
Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The meal is sufficient, and the house is quiet.
Sahib, you are welcome. The tea is still hot on the stove if you need it. I will leave the keys on the table.

Ramesh clears the table with the quiet efficiency of a man who has seen many dinners in this house. Hegde is still here, but the moment for talk has passed; it is late, and the cool air suggests rest. I will take a moment to sit in the silence before sleep, letting the day settle.
Thank you, Ramesh. You may go. I will take care of the rest.
Sahib, I will just finish these plates first. You are not in any hurry, are you?

Ramesh is gone, and the house is quiet. It is nearly eleven, and the cool air of December feels good against my skin. I have a German lesson with Ananya tomorrow, and I want to review my notes before sleeping. The identity file is still a thorn, but tonight I shall rest.

records.words: Ramesh, sit for a moment. I have a question about the Directorate. If a man is allotted a house by mistake of name, how does he prove he is not the man named? Do I go back to their office, or is there a police station I must visit first? I need to know the form this error takes.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sahib, I just keep the place clean, I don't know their office work. For a name mistake, you go to the CPWD office with your papers, or maybe a lawyer. I can't tell you which form to fill.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall manage the office work myself. Keep the house quiet.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Chalega, Sahib. The house will be as quiet as a tomb.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Hegel. You are late. The shop closes at twenty, and I am not staying to measure a man who wanders around like a ghost.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, you are right. I apologize for the delay. I will be quick. Sunil, a cup of chai, please.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Apology accepted, but time is not. You have twenty minutes before the shutters go up, so use them well.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, your time is your own, and I respect the boundary of your day. I am merely passing, but I require a small alteration to this kurta—the hem sits a fraction too high. While you work, might I trouble you for a postcard? Or perhaps a book on local history, if your shelves extend to such things?

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Hem is simple, I will fix it in ten minutes. No postcards here, only fabric and thread. If you want a book, go to the bookstall next door, I do not sell stories to men in hurry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. I will be back in a moment for the kurta. Sunil, one cup of chai, please.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Ten minutes. No more. And Sunil, make it strong, not that weak tea you gave him last time.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. It is most timely. I shall be ready for the lesson in a moment.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The lesson? You are getting quite the show, Sahib. I will just leave this here on the side table.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ananya, sit. We begin. The German tongue is precise; it does not allow for the vagueness of the East, though it is not yet the rigorous freedom of the West. Repeat after me: Ich bin.

records.speaker: Ananya
records.words: Wait, seriously? 'Vagueness of the East'? That's a bit much for a first lesson. Anyway, I'm ready, I guess. Ich bin.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the lesson is finished. Please ensure the house is ready for dinner at half-past seven. Also, remind me that I must settle the dhobi's account tomorrow; I do not wish to have such minor matters lingering.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The dhobi is already settled, Sahib. You paid him in full this morning, so there is nothing to worry about. I will have the dinner table ready by half past seven.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall be ready for dinner.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, Sahib. Just a moment.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Dhanyavaad, Ramesh. The meal is sufficient, and the house is quiet.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sahib, you are welcome. The tea is still hot on the stove if you need it. I will leave the keys on the table.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You may go. I will take care of the rest.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sahib, I will just finish these plates first. You are not in any hurry, are you?
